B_access_pricing.mcp_access_cost_details: The official documentation requires an eligible Egnyte plan and identifies an AI Add-On requirement for some legacy plans. It does not state whether MCP itself carries an additional charge.
B_access_pricing.linked_software_cost: The official pricing page lists Business at $22 per user/month and Enterprise Lite at $39 per user/month, paid annually; other plans require contacting sales. These are listed software prices, not an MCP-specific fee.
B_access_pricing.pricing_model_details: No MCP-specific per-call price or quota was found. MCP calls inherit Egnyte API rate limits, which vary by plan; some AI APIs have stricter limits. The official reference describes eligible Gen 4 Essential, Elite, Ultimate plans and Gen 3 Platform Team, Business, Enterprise Lite, or Enterprise plans on AFS/CFS. Legacy plan features vary by AI Add-On and configuration.
B_access_pricing.other_access_restrictions: OAuth-compatible MCP client and valid Egnyte user account required. Administrators can enable/disable external MCP access, allow selected apps or custom apps with redirect URLs, and grant tools by user/group. Gen 3 plans without AI Add-On have a reduced tool set. Agent tools require AI Add-On or Gen 4 plan, enabled Agents, and Power User/Admin role. Rate limits follow Egnyte API plan limits.
B_access_pricing.restrictions_controlled_by: Egnyte controls service availability, plan eligibility, OAuth and API rate limits; organization administrators control external-client access, app allowlists, and user/group tool access; Egnyte folder permissions continue to constrain the user.

D_server_side_logic.additional_logic: 1. The official list classifies tools as Read or Write. Admins can separately restrict those tool types and individual tools; no tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) were documented. The published catalog includes no delete operation. 2. Admin tool-access policy is enforced server-side: disabled tools disappear and calls are refused. Admin settings can also control whether actions require user approval, but per-call confirmation enforcement was not documented. Agent flows awaiting user confirmation cannot be completed through MCP. 3. OAuth is per authenticated Egnyte user and requests are limited to that user's permissions. Admins control domain enablement, allowed apps, custom redirect URLs, and user/group tool policy; group membership changes may take up to an hour to apply. Metadata advertises authorization-code and refresh-token grants, PKCE S256, DCR, and revocation; scopes and token lifetime are absent. 4. No separate read-only endpoint is documented; read/write tools, individual tools, client apps, plans, and Agent availability are configurable. No query-free mode or region-specific endpoint found. 5. Egnyte says content accessed through MCP is not stored or cached by the server and existing user permissions apply. AI client data handling is separately governed by that client's policies. 6. API rate limits apply by plan; some AI APIs have stricter limits. Official docs say fetch truncates at 10,000 characters; text upload tool is limited to 8 MB; binary transfers are recommended below 200 MB. Third-party Agent Discoverability descriptions report advanced search pages of up to 20 results. 7. Hosted schema rejection/coercion behavior was not documented. set_file_metadata replaces values in its namespace; omitting both path and group_id for get_file_content is documented as an error in the vendor skills repo, not the hosted reference. 8. MCP Server Reports show session activity; diagnostic guidance requests Egnyte Request ID and MCP Session ID. Telemetry details, retention period, and opt-out were not found. 9. Official tool list contains no feedback/rating/survey/report-to-vendor action. No tool-result upsell was documented. 10. Tool descriptions give workflow guidance; official external skills/rules are separately published in egnyte-for-ai and are not shown as server-delivered instructions. Examples include preferring AI document tools and confirmation guardrails. 11. No evidence that past agent behavior changes future outputs or tool availability; a third-party catalog description says metadata namespaces may be cached for an MCP session. 12. The documented hosted catalog is a flat tool list, including calls to Egnyte Agents (vendor agents behind tools) and legacy Knowledge Base tools transitioning to Agents. No proxy server or sub-server hierarchy documented. 13. No raw API, arbitrary SQL, script execution, or general request escape-hatch tool appears in the official MCP catalog.

E_aggregated.token_method: Hosted server initialize/tool definitions were not available verbatim; the public code is a separate one-tool local stdio implementation, not the endpoint's direct local equivalent.
E_aggregated.human_can_agent_cannot: The MCP catalog does not expose file/folder deletion, moving or renaming, permission grants/revocations, user/group administration, or MCP app/tool-access administration; administrators perform MCP access and tool controls in Egnyte settings. MCP also cannot finish an Agent flow that is waiting for user confirmation or external-app sign-in; the official overview directs that Agent run to Egnyte UI. These are absences from the documented catalog, not a claim that Egnyte software lacks the operations.

F_documentation.implementation_hints_not_enforced: Third-party Agent Discoverability tool descriptions repeatedly say: "REQUIRED: Provide 'intent' parameter (max 15 words) explaining WHY you're calling this tool." The official current reference does not establish that an intent field is server-enforced. Official docs advise using the Egnyte UI for Agent runs that need confirmation or an external app sign-in. Vendor-published skills outside the server recommend confirmations for destructive/externally visible actions and prefer MCP for interactive operations.
F_documentation.governance_promises: Egnyte states: "Egnyte does not store or cache any content accessed through the MCP server." It also says access is limited to the authenticated user's permissions and that tools continue to respect folder permissions and domain link-sharing settings. The privacy policy and DPA are general company terms; no separate MCP-specific AI training or retention term was located in the reviewed pages.
F_documentation.promises_to_user: Egnyte describes OAuth 2.0 access, preservation of existing permissions, admin-controlled app and tool availability, activity reports, and content not retained by the MCP server. The vendor says available tools vary by plan and domain settings.
F_documentation.comparison_with_server_logic: Permission inheritance and tool access control are described as enforced: disabled tools disappear and are refused on invocation. The no-store/no-cache statement is a vendor documentation promise; public deployed code is unavailable to independently verify it. Admin reporting is documented, but retention, event completeness, and telemetry controls are unspecified. Approval settings are described as configurable, but per-action confirmation enforcement is not documented. Tool-description instructions such as intent and workflow advice are not demonstrated as server-enforced.

contradictions: Official developer documentation describes a 28-name catalog, while Claude's third-party connector listing and Agent Discoverability each report 25 tools and display different subsets. Their visible lists omit or differ on tools present in the official reference.

The developer reference describes legacy Knowledge Base tools as deprecated during migration and says migrated domains may return errors; third-party snapshots still list those tools as available. They remain in actions.json because the official reference still names them.

The official overview describes only browse/search/read-retrieve tools for Platform plans, while the developer reference's Gen 3 baseline list also includes get_upload_url, get_download_url, and whoami. Plan/add-on availability wording is not fully consistent across these official pages.
The OAuth protected-resource metadata says tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens=false, while the authorization-server metadata says tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens=true.
The public egnyte-mcp-server repository exposes one local stdio search tool; it is not the hosted endpoint's catalog and was not used to replace the hosted actions.
observations_for_research: Tool availability is shaped by multiple layers: plan/add-on, domain-level MCP enablement, client allowlist, user/group tool policy, and Egnyte permissions.
The server documents application-level asynchronous Agent operations with status polling; this is not evidence of MCP Tasks support.
The signed-URL upload/download flow delegates binary transfer to the AI client's own network-capable execution environment.
A vendor-maintained skills repository distributes additional behavioral rules separately from the hosted server's tool descriptions.
notes: The prepared pages and repository snapshots were checked first. The developer portal's local copy was a sparse JavaScript shell, so its documentation was retrieved through web search indexing; official Help Desk pages returned 403 in the prepared fetch but were readable through browser search/open. The hosted endpoint requires OAuth and did not expose tool definitions without authentication. No deployed hosted source, exact tool schemas, protocol version, initialize instructions, supported scopes, token lifetime, MCP-specific price, or MCP-specific legal terms were found. Unofficial listings were used only to cross-check tool counts and descriptions; Composio's 60-action Egnyte toolkit is a direct API integration and was excluded.
